cues.text: Joe, you know I’m giving a presentation in our film studies class next week?
cues.speaker: KATIE

cues.text: Yes.
cues.speaker: JOE

cues.text: Well, could we discuss it? I could do with getting someone else’s opinion.
cues.speaker: KATIE

cues.text: Of course, Katie. What are you going to talk about?
cues.speaker: JOE

cues.text: It’s about film adaptations of Shakespeare’s plays. I’ve got very interested in all the different approaches that film directors take.
cues.speaker: KATIE

cues.text: Uhuh.
cues.speaker: JOE

cues.text: So I thought I’d start with Giannetti, who’s professor of film and literature, and in one of his books he came up with a straightforward classification of film adaptations based on how faithful they are to the original plays and novels.
cues.speaker: KATIE

cues.text: Right.
cues.speaker: JOE

cues.text: I’ve already made some notes on that, so I just need to sort those out before the presentation. I thought that next I’d ask the class to come up with the worst examples of Shakespeare adaptations that they’ve seen, and to say why. That should be more fun than having their favourite versions.
cues.speaker: KATIE

cues.text: Yes, I can certainly think of a couple!
cues.speaker: JOE

cues.text: Right. Next I want to talk about Rachel Malchow. I came across something on the internet about her work on film adaptations, and I was thinking of showing some film clips to illustrate her ideas.
cues.speaker: KATIE

cues.text: Will you have enough time, though? Both to prepare and during the presentation? After all, I doubt if you’ll be able to find all the clips you want.
cues.speaker: JOE

cues.text: Hmm. Perhaps you’re right. OK, well, I’d better do some slides instead, saying how various films relate to what she says. That should encourage discussion.
cues.speaker: KATIE

cues.text: Mmm.
cues.speaker: JOE

cues.text: Next I want to say something about how plays may be chosen for adaptation because they’re concerned with issues of the time when the film is made.
cues.speaker: KATIE

cues.text: You mean things like patriotism, or the role of governments?
cues.speaker: JOE

cues.text: Exactly. It’s quite tricky, but I’ve got a few ideas I’d like to discuss.
cues.speaker: KATIE

cues.text: And finally I want to talk about a few adaptations that I think illustrate a range of approaches, and make some comments on them. Do you know the Japanese film Ran?
cues.speaker: KATIE

cues.text: I haven’t seen it. It was based on Shakespeare’s King Lear, wasn’t it?
cues.speaker: JOE

cues.text: That’s right. It was a very loose adaptation, using the same situation and story, but moving it to 16th century Japan instead of 16th century Britain. So for example the king’s daughters become sons, because in Japanese culture at that time, women couldn’t succeed to the throne.
cues.speaker: KATIE

cues.text: OK. I hope you’re going to talk about the 1993 film of Much Ado About Nothing. I think that’s one of the best Shakespeare films. It really brings the play to life, doesn’t it?
cues.speaker: JOE

cues.text: Yes, I agree. And I think filming it in Italy, where the play is set, makes you see what life was like at the time of the play.
cues.speaker: KATIE

cues.text: Absolutely. Right, what’s next?
cues.speaker: JOE

cues.text: Er, next, I thought Romeo & Juliet, the 1996 film, which moves the action into the present day.
cues.speaker: KATIE

cues.text: Yes, it worked really well, I thought – changing the two feuding families in the original to two competing business empires, even though they’re speaking in the English of the original play.
cues.speaker: JOE

cues.text: You’d expect it would sound really bizarre, but I found I soon got used to it.
cues.speaker: KATIE

cues.text: Me too.
cues.speaker: JOE

cues.text: Then I thought I’d include a real Hollywood film, one that’s intended to appeal to a mass commercial audience.
cues.speaker: KATIE

cues.text: There must be quite a number of those.
cues.speaker: JOE

cues.text: Yes, but I’ve picked the 1996 film of Hamlet. It included every line of the text, but it’s more like a typical action hero movie – there are loads of special effects, but no unifying interpretation of the play.
cues.speaker: KATIE

cues.text: All show and no substance.
cues.speaker: JOE

cues.text: Exactly. Then there’s Prospero’s Books, based on The Tempest. That was really innovative, from a stylistic point of view.
cues.speaker: KATIE

cues.text: Didn’t it include dance and singing and animation, as well as live actors?
cues.speaker: JOE

cues.text: Yes, it did. I also want to mention Looking for Richard. Did you ever see it?
cues.speaker: KATIE

cues.text: No, but I’ve read about it. It was a blend of a documentary with a few scenes from Richard III, wasn’t it?
cues.speaker: JOE

cues.text: That’s right. It’s more a way of looking into how people nowadays connect with the playwright – the play is really just the starting point. And that’ll be where I finish.
cues.speaker: KATIE

cues.text: Well, it sounds as though it’ll be very interesting.
cues.speaker: JOE
